content.thinking:
I need to write this file carefully in one pass without testing, so I'm planning out realistic proportions for the monster truck pixel art first—tire diameter, overall width, length, height—then working out wheel placement with specific radius and axle positions.

For the skeleton, I'm setting up a chassis root joint with child hinge joints for each wheel, separate steering joints for the front wheels, and hinge joints for the doors, keeping the hierarchy simple and consistent. I'm working through the tire and tread geometry, building cylinder shapes for tires and planning lug nut details as small boxes ringed around each wheel, merged per wheel bone for efficiency.

Working out lug placement math...

Now I'm figuring out wheel and tire radii so everything sits flush on the floor, plus planning rim and hub details like lug nuts, center caps, and sidewall texture accents.

Still writing pixel texture generator...

Writing tire paint logic...

For the chassis, I'm sketching the truck body as a cab, hood, and bed in a red-orange paint scheme, considering panel textures with metallic base and flame decals using a tiled box approach.

Now I'm planning the undercarriage: frame rails along the length, axles with differentials, and suspension made from angled shock rods, coil springs built from stacked rings, and four-link bars connecting axle to frame, followed by positioning the hood and cab sections of the body.

Then I'm working out the body height and width relative to the wheels, setting the body to sit on mounting posts above the chassis rails so it clears the tires, roughly 2 units wide to stay slightly outside the tire width.

I'm adding flared fender boxes above the wheel wells for a stylized monster-truck silhouette, then starting to block out the body itself as stepped box shapes -- a hood section sloping toward a pixel-textured grille at the front.

Now I'm building the cab and greenhouse: a lower cab box, an upper greenhouse box slightly narrower, and pixel-textured glass decals on the front, sides, and rear faces to simulate windows with a blue dithered highlight, leaving gaps between them to imply pillars, topped with a wide roof slab.

I'm adding the truck bed as a hollow structure with floor, side walls, tailgate, and front wall, plus a roll bar, chrome exhaust stacks behind the cab, and front/rear bumpers with a brush guard, glowing headlights, a light bar, and a winch, while settling on the body's base paint color.

Writing flame decal texture...

I work out the camera orientation math to confirm that for the +X side, the front faces the viewer's left, while for the -X side it's mirrored so front faces right — this tells me how to orient the flame/plane geometry per side.

So I'll build the texture generation with a flip parameter so flames and windows mirror correctly on each side. For door roundels, I want to avoid directional numbers since mirroring would flip them oddly, so I'm leaning toward a symmetric digit like "8" or "0" rather than something like "9" that reads wrong reversed.

A skull emblem is perfect since it's naturally symmetric -- I'll draw a pixel skull for the hood and door roundels, which also fits the monster truck aesthetic well. Skipping any text banners since SVG text isn't available here.

Now I'm planning the joint hierarchy: chassis as the root spine, then wheelFL/FR/RL/RR as hinge joints, steering hinges for front wheels, door hinges, and a tailgate hinge, with each door panel positioned at its hinge location along the cab's side.

I'm working out door placement as thin slab panels that sit flush against a narrower cab core, with hinge joints oriented vertically at the front edge of each door for rotation, while wheel joints get axles running along the x-axis and steering joints pivot vertically at the kingpin, with wheels as child parts attached at the wheel center.

Each joint definition needs a position plus parent reference, with hinge and steer joints layered so the wheel attaches to the steering bone at the same location. I'm checking wheel spacing across the axle to get the total width right, then moving into the tread lug geometry for each wheel.

Writing lug generation code...

Adding sidewall bead rim geometry and decal placement...

Simplifying: rim cylinder goes to ±0.376 and decal sits at 0.381 to avoid z-fighting with the 2mm gap. I'll add lug nuts as small cylinders in a ring, beadlock bolts around the rim, and use chrome color "#c9ccd4" for the metal parts.

For wheel orientation I'm flipping decal direction left vs right while keeping the texture roughly symmetric. For the tyre decal, I'll use a plane with a transparent-cut texture instead of a circle geometry, letting alpha below 0.5 define the disc edge so it matches the drawn texture grid.

Now I'm laying out concentric regions by pixel distance from center: an outer dark tread edge, a shoulder band with dashed notches, and a sidewall band with alternating lettering dashes based on angle.

I'm filling in the tire's inner zones—a yellow accent ring, pseudo-text lettering, an inner bead, and a chrome rim band with bolt dots at regular angles—then shaping the hub with a dark inner dish and spoke pattern.

Now I'm adding the center cap, lug nuts positioned at even angular intervals, and setting up a shading helper using pixel distance and angle from center with Bayer dithering for a lit-from-above chrome look, before assigning final colors to the red body and black trim.

Then I'm defining the chassis rails as steel boxes flanking the wheels, with darker crossmembers spaced along the frame, followed by the front axle tube and hub stubs built as rods spanning between the wheel positions.

I'm figuring out the differential housing as a sphere colored a brassy yellow-orange, and setting the front and rear axle z-positions so the wheelbase and tire gaps work out proportionally. I'm then checking that the body length clears the tire overhangs front and rear, extending the hood and bumper and tail sections so nothing clips the big wheels.

Now I'm designing the shocks at each corner, placing rods between the axle and chassis shock towers with a yellow coil-wrapped look, considering whether to sweep a true helical spring or approximate it with stacked discs for simplicity.

Adding small post boxes as body mounts connecting the rail to the shock tower, then planning four-link suspension bars as thin rods from the axle.

Still placing rods and parts...

Now I'm sketching the body shell itself—starting with the floor pan, rocker panels, and a front clip box that will anchor the hood and fenders together.

I'm then adding the hood details: a raised scoop with intake texture, plus a decal stripe placed on the hood's top face, working out the local axis orientation needed so the plane aligns flush against the upward-facing hood surface.

With up [0,0,1], the cross product gives -X, so with the front-up orientation on screen, model's right matches -X, confirming the texture is unmirrored correctly. Now I'm working out the grille placement on the front face, computing the texture plane's orientation so the u-axis maps to +X and figuring out how that appears to a viewer facing the front.

I'm laying out the grille texture with black background and chrome vertical bars, plus headlights as glowing yellow-white boxes on either side and lower fog lights. Then I'm adding the chrome bumper, vertical and horizontal guard rods, red tow hooks, and a winch box tucked behind the bumper.

For the fenders, I'm sketching painted flare boxes above the front and rear wheels with black lip trim underneath and hanging mud flaps near the rear tires in black and yellow. Now I'm shaping the cab as a box sized to sit just above the hood.

For the greenhouse section above the cab, I'm working out a tapered frustum shape for the windshield, figuring out which axis controls width versus height as the shape slopes upward and back, then setting the start and end sections to taper the glass area appropriately.

Working through the frustum geometry, I check the base and top centers independently: base depth 1.5 centered near 0.1, top depth 0.95 centered near -0.1, giving a good rake on the front edge but a nearly vertical rear edge. The issue is the box ends come out square rather than following that taper naturally.

Since manually tilting flat ends creates unwanted sloped roof faces, I switch strategy: I'll build the greenhouse by extruding a 2D side-view outline (in the z-y plane) across the x-axis thickness. This avoids the tilt problem entirely and gives a clean cross-section shape, with the extrusion centered properly along the thickness axis.

Actually, this gives me an idea to do the entire vehicle body the same way—extrude a full side-profile outline covering the hood, cab, and bed in one shape, with window decals and paint applied to the flat side faces afterward.

Mapping out the rear-bottom edge then up through the front face, hood slope, and into the windshield base point by point.

Still refining the body outline...

Working out the roof span and side silhouette dimensions, checking where the window quad edges fall relative to the cab's sloped front at different y-heights.

Mapping out pixel placement for the sloped window edge per row, then planning the glass gradient colors with diagonal highlight streaks and black pillar columns for the frame.

Now I'm computing the windshield and rear window decal planes—figuring slope lengths, texture resolution, and surface normals so the glass textures align correctly with each sloped panel, along with the UV directions for mapping.

For the roof I'm adding a light bar box with glowing yellow segments on the front face, plus roof vents and an antenna rod to give the vehicle more detail up top.

Checking total height with the light bar and antenna comes out around 3.7m, which matches real monster truck proportions reasonably well. Now I'm moving to body paint, extruding paint cells along the side faces with normal variations, including a darker tone near the lower sill for shading.

Writing paint shader logic...

Still defining bed geometry...

I'll add chrome roll bar hoops with a diagonal brace and small round lights mounted on top facing forward, then place angled exhaust stacks just behind the cab with clamp rings and a flared tip. For the doors, I'm sketching a slab panel sized to the cab's lower region.

I'm now working out the door placement more precisely, recessing it slightly from the body surface and adding a chrome handle, while planning where flame decals should sit across the door and fender without colliding with the door's protruding edge.

I realize the flame decal region overlaps the door and would move incorrectly with it, so I need to restrict flames to the front clip only and keep the roundel decal bound to the door's own bone so it moves correctly with the door joint.

Still defining flame height function...

Working out the flame tip shape so the steep rise is on the right and slow taper on the left, then shading each pixel by its relative height into inner white-yellow, mid yellow, and outer orange bands with a dark red outline, mirroring the x-coordinate for the opposite side.

I realize the fender flare geometry overlaps the flame decal plane near the front wheel, partially hiding it, so I'm reconsidering the flare's size and position—maybe thinner, raised, or arch-shaped—to keep it clear of the decal.

Then I'm planning the hood details: a black scoop box with a dark grille texture on its front face, plus considering adding a chrome supercharger blower on top of the hood for that monster truck engine look.

Placing yellow strap boxes, then positioning a skull decal on the hood front, accounting for the slight slope of the hood surface so it sits flush without clipping the blower.

Now I'm laying out the front end: dual headlight squares with chrome bezels and glowing cores, a black mesh grille plate with a textured decal, and a chrome front bumper with tow-hooks, fog lamps, and a skid plate sized to clear the tires. I'm mirroring this with a rear bumper and planning red tailgate lights.

For the back I'm adding glowing rear light boxes, a chrome tow hitch ball, and a license plate plane positioned on the tailgate. I'm working out the correct right-vector orientation for someone viewing the plate from behind the vehicle so any lettering reads correctly, then sketching a minimal pixel-font approach to stamp a few characters like "M," "X," "1," and "7" onto the plate instead of full text.

Settling on a simple plate reading "700" using a 3x5 pixel glyph scheme for the digits, then moving to design small running-board steps on each side positioned to clear the tire wells and cab area.

Now I'm adding mirrors (a rod arm plus a small box mirror on each side), chrome door handles, and thin dark gap lines marking the door edges to add surface detail to the body.

For finishing touches I'm considering hood pins and latches but deciding to skip most of them, then designing a skull roundel decal for each door as a symmetric 16x16 pixel pattern in black, white, and yellow placed centrally on the door panel.

Still laying out the skull pixel grid...

I continue building out the remaining rows for the nose, mouth, and teeth sections, verifying each sums to 16 columns, then decide to skip the crossbones detail and pad the design to a 16x14 grid overall.

Now I'm setting up the color palette with black outlines and bone-white fill against the red body, reusing the skull texture for the hood emblem and a smaller door roundel. I add random mud speckling near the bottom of the tyres and chassis for weathering, then move on to building the roof light bar with a mounting base and five small light boxes positioned along the front edge.

I'm sketching out a gearbox and axle tube detail under the chassis, considering steel-colored tubes and yellow sphere-shaped diff covers, while deciding to skip sidepipes and keep the glass windows solid rather than showing any interior.

Adding bolt rings and axle hub stubs...

I'm deciding to skip the portal axle gear boxes to keep things simpler, and instead planning how wheel parts get bone-assigned, with tyre and hub caps under each wheel joint so front wheel parts stay children of the steering bone.

Now I'm also reviewing imports to only pull in what's actually used, since TypeScript's strict unused-locals setting will flag anything extra. I'm sketching out a box helper function that creates parts attached to a bone with position, size, and color, starting from a chassis joint as the default parent.

I'm defining typed Fill, Joint, and Paint imports, then building a decal plane helper that creates textured planes attached to a bone with optional direction, up vector, and glow effect applied afterward.

Now I'm designing the tyre face texture generator, mapping polar coordinates across a 40x40 pixel grid to render shoulder notches, sidewall dithering, lettering patterns, and a yellow sidewall ring based on radial distance bands.

Still writing texture code...

Checking that flame texture mapping and the radial boundary math line up at the right scale. Now I'm sketching out the other texture functions needed: window sides, windshield, rear, grille, skull decal, plate, lights, hood scoop, and bed liner.

For the bed, I'm designing a ridged pixel texture to simulate a liner floor and mapping it onto the box geometry with a fine texel size, applying it across all faces. For the chassis rails I'll stick with plain paint, and I'm defining a steel cell-paint pattern that mixes several gray-blue tones based on surface normal and some randomness for a brushed metal look.

I'm now setting up a yellow paint variant with a similar dithered gradient across tan-to-bright-yellow tones for axles and drivetrain parts, plus a chrome paint for the exhaust and bumper. Writing mud texture logic...

Still building wheel parts...

Placing lug nuts around the ring and rotating cylinder geometry to align with the axle, merging them into one mesh. I'm skipping the brake rotor detail for now, and moving on to defining steering joints for the front wheels as hinge points on the chassis.

Now I'm setting up the doors with hinge joints on either side of the chassis, adding door slabs, handles, and roundels as child parts, then working out the tailgate's hinge joint and orientation at the rear.

Now I'm working out the tailgate geometry: a box sized roughly 1.8x0.4x0.1 positioned at the back of the body, attached to a tailgate bone, fitting between the bed's inner side walls which sit at about x=±0.85 given 0.1-thick walls at x=±0.9. I'm placing a plate on the gate to match this 1.7-wide opening.

I'm hinging the tailgate at its bottom edge and sizing the bed floor and side wall boxes to fit the cargo area, then skipping wheel wells and extra lighting as unnecessary detail. For the antenna, I'm adding a thin rod with a small pennant-shaped flag extruded near its tip for a bit of character.

I'm deciding to keep the color palette focused on red, yellow, and black rather than adding underglow accents, estimating the total part count lands around 200, which feels reasonable. Now I'm starting to extrude the main body shape from its outline coordinates.

Writing extrude call...

Checking the windshield decal positioning against the body's edge at x=±0.95, confirming its width and height fit the slanted glass plane centered around the midpoint of the slope.

Now checking the windshield texture sizing against width/height ratios, then working out the rear window dimensions and center position from the slope between its corner points.

I'm designing a glass texture generator function that handles slant angles, mirroring, and pillar placement for the windows.

Writing texture generator logic...

Working out the slant direction for each face so the window taper looks correct from both viewing sides, mapping texture coordinates differently depending on whether it's the +X or -X face.

Now I'm sketching out the remaining textures: the windshield with a chrome visor strip and frame border, a grille texture with vertical chrome bars and a yellow diamond emblem, a small license plate, and keeping other details like mudflaps and hood vents simple flat colors to save effort. Moving on to composing the actual mesh code, including lug nuts and wheel geometry.

I'm figuring out the shocks and springs: stacking torus segments into coiled springs around a shock rod, colored red-orange, with yellow rod bodies, then positioning four shocks at the corners of the vehicle while considering whether to split them into pairs per axle.

Now I'm placing the suspension link bars connecting the axle to the chassis, angling them inward toward center based on whether the axle is front or rear, and starting on the drive shaft rod connecting the axle pumpkin to the chassis.

Then I'm checking that the drive shaft and transfer case box don't collide with other components, confirming the engine stays hidden, and sizing mud flaps as small boxes positioned behind each wheel with black coloring and a yellow stripe, hanging low enough to clear the wheel well but short enough not to drag.

I'm also starting to plan the front fender flares, working out their z-range placement relative to the wheel center.

I'm sweeping chrome roll-hoop tubes using polyline paths attached to the chassis bone, placing one hoop near z=-1.0 with corner points defining its rectangular frame, and considering a second hoop plus longitudinal rods connecting the hoop tops to the cab.

Now I'm adding diagonal cross-brace rods between hoop corners, then planning round light pods on the hoop front face—chrome rings with glowing lens discs positioned across the hoop width, facing forward.

Next I'm placing exhaust stacks between the hoop and cab, tapering upward so they poke above the roofline, with clamp rings at a few heights and a tapered tip. I'm checking total vehicle height stays reasonable with the antenna and stacks factored in before moving on to the hood.

Now I'm adding hood details: a chrome blower box floating slightly above the hood surface, a black scoop sitting on top, and a few velocity stacks protruding from the scoop to suggest an engine intake.

Then I'm adding yellow drive-belt bands wrapping around the blower housing for visual detail, and considering a skull decal on the hood front, though I'm noting its texel size doesn't match the rest of the texturing scheme.

Working out the skull decal scale—matching its pixel density to the flame decals so everything reads consistently—and positioning it on both the hood front and the door, checking that it fits within the panel dimensions. Now I'm sizing the flame decals along the front fenders based on the available surface length.

For the side flames, I'm computing texture dimensions and placement so the decal sits above the black rocker line and below the hood top edge, then handling the texture flip so the flame orientation mirrors correctly between the left and right sides.

I need to check that the flame decal doesn't overlap the door roundel or hinge area, then I'll add the black panel gap lines and door handle details, and sketch out the mirror geometry as a rod, housing box, and small chrome glass insert mounted near the front of the body.

Next I'm adding running boards as dark steel boxes along the body sides, double-checking the step placement clears the front tire, and noting that bumper and linkage details are already coded while radiator hoses and decals can be skipped. I'll also add a black visor strip above the roofline.

Now I'm positioning a roof-mounted light bar with glowing lamp boxes just behind the visor, finishing the layout before returning the root object and wrapping everything in the exported build function. Finally I'm tallying up the joints: chassis, four wheels, two steering joints, two doors, and the tailgate.

Setting up imports and type definitions, then defining color palette constants and paint objects for the truck's materials...

Still writing wheel geometry...

Checking lug spacing confirms gaps between the 14 lugs are fine, and the lugs stay embedded within the tyre radius. Now I'm wondering whether paint baking on the merged geometry needs UV coordinates, since part-level painting typically relies on position and normal data.

Positioning the five spoke nuts around each wheel using small rotated cylinders placed at calculated angles. I'm setting up a reusable box-creation helper function...

Adding cylinder and decal helpers...

Positioning the plate decal against the gate's rear face, checking rear tyre and bumper clearances, and fixing the door window decal to attach to the body rather than the door itself.

Sizing the tyre face decal to match the rim radius and placing it just outside the tyre face to avoid z-fighting with the rim cylinder, while skipping a torus bulge for the sidewall as unnecessary detail.

Checking texel density for the paint atlas against the total painted surface area across lugs and tyres, estimating around 1cm texels are enough to cover roughly 70-150 m² of geometry at a 1024 resolution, so I'll stick with that size rather than bumping to 2048 or 4096.

I'll keep lugs flat dark ("#1b1a1f") and limit mud to the tyre cylinder itself, since the tread is mostly hidden. The sidewall mud could instead come from a decal layer.

I'm adding mud speckles to the lower half of the decal texture using a deterministic hash function on pixel coordinates to decide which spots get splattered, with probability increasing toward the bottom edge. I'm restructuring the fill logic so the base face color is computed first, then mud brown overrides it for the selected speckled pixels.

Now I'm writing the flame texture generator, defining tongue shapes across rows where amplitude decays from front to back, with color bands shifting from pale yellow at the tip through orange-yellow to deep orange, plus a dark red outline at the top edge of each tongue.

For the glass texture, I'm building a function that slants the window edge based on row position, draws dark frame borders and an optional pillar divider, then fills the interior with a gradient-like tint using a banded pattern and dithered glass color picks.

I'm defining the rear window and windshield using this glass texture with different sizes, then moving to a grille texture that frames a chrome border, adds vertical bars, and stamps a yellow diamond badge in the center. Now I'm starting a license plate texture with a cream background and blue border frame, about to stamp text onto it.

Working out digit pixel patterns for the plate numbers, laying out "700" as a 3x5 grid per digit with spacing, verifying each row's character count adds up to the plate width before stamping them in dark pixels.

Now I'm designing a noisy liner texture with speckled grays and a bayer-dithered pattern, then fixing the tile sizing so the box's texels match its face proportions instead of stretching. I'm also setting up a skull texture palette and planning to build chrome shock absorbers with rods at each corner of the chassis.

Working out shock tower placement, spring posts, and rail alignment to avoid collisions...

After the chassis, I'm adding a front bumper guard with vertical and horizontal chrome rods, checking that they don't fully obscure the headlights or grille positioning.

Now adding fog lights on the bumper face, a skid plate under the hood, and double-checking the chassis rail lengths line up correctly under the bumper. I'm setting up the wheel attachment function with steering joints for the front, defining door hinge joints with left/right naming, and making sure the color types align with the part function signatures before finalizing the tailgate hinge joint and writing everything out.
